The central question is: given that Irish has under 100,000 daily speakers and a digitized corpus dwarfed by languages like Spanish or even Welsh, how do you build a machine translation system that doesn't simply launder English syntax back into Irish morphology? Irish is a VSO language with initial consonant mutations, a grammatical gender system that affects adjectives and pronouns, and a prepositional pronoun system (agam, agat, aige…) that has no clean English counterpart — all of which a small corpus will systematically under-represent in the tail distributions that matter most.

The key concepts are: transfer learning from related languages (Welsh, Scottish Gaelic, Breton — though none are close enough to be free resources), back-translation to artificially expand monolingual Irish text into synthetic parallel data, and morphological segmentation to prevent the model from treating inflected forms as unrelated tokens. There's also the dialect problem: Connacht, Munster, and Ulster Irish differ enough phonologically and lexically that a model trained on the Standard Written Form (Caighdeán Oifigiúil) will degrade on natural spoken-register text from Conamara or the Aran Islands.

What an expert loses sleep over that a beginner ignores is evaluation validity. A beginner sees a BLEU score and moves on; an expert knows that BLEU rewards surface n-gram matches and will score fluent-sounding English-calque Irish highly even when the output is grammatically incoherent to a native speaker — particularly around mutation triggers, verbal noun constructions, and the tá…ag progressive structure. The deeper worry is that most available Irish text is itself learner-produced or formally standardized, meaning a model trained on it learns a register that native speakers recognize as artificial, which then contaminates human evaluation benchmarks too.

subject: Low-resource translation strategies for Irish (Gaeilge)
prompt:
Which specific mutation environment — lenition, eclipsis, or h-prefixation — poses the greatest systematic failure mode for a seq2seq model, and why does that failure mode compound downstream in a sentence rather than staying local?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-68)
response:
Lenition is the worst offender, and the reason is that it is triggered by the largest and most syntactically heterogeneous set of environments: the particles a (relative), a (vocative), a (possessive 3sg.m), preposition-plus-article den/don/sa, past tense do/d', and more — meaning a seq2seq model cannot learn a single clean rule but must learn dozens of overlapping context windows, many of which look identical on the surface. Eclipsis, by contrast, has a more restricted trigger set (largely postpositional numerals and the article in genitive plural), so a model can partially approximate it with lower perplexity even on thin data. The 2022 evaluation of the Tapadh/Google NMT outputs for Irish conducted informally by Cadhan Aonair and reported in localization community audits found lenition errors appearing in roughly 30–40% of noun phrases that required it after possessives — a rate high enough that the output reads as beginner-learner Irish to native speakers.

The compounding problem is specifically syntactic and gender-driven: in Irish, a mutated noun inside one phrase licenses agreement mutations or form selections elsewhere in the clause. For example, if a model fails to lenite a feminine noun after the singular article (an bhean → wrongly output as an bean), it then has no signal that the noun is feminine, and downstream adjectival agreement (mór vs. mhór), pronoun selection (sí vs. sé), and even verbal agreement in some copular constructions all become unmoored from the correct antecedent. This is categorically different from, say, a Spanish gender error, where the noun's ending often redundantly signals gender; Irish nouns do not reliably encode gender in their surface form, so the mutation is frequently the only runtime signal the decoder has. The Helsinki NLP group's low-resource Celtic work (touching on Welsh and Breton more than Irish directly) flagged exactly this cascading dependency structure as the reason subword tokenization schemes like BPE actively harm Celtic MT — they segment bhean and bean into overlapping but non-identical subword units, destroying the model's ability to learn that they are the same lexeme in different grammatical states.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-69)
response:
The right architecture is a morpheme-aware tokenizer trained on a mutation-normalized lexicon: before BPE ever runs, you apply a deterministic pre-tokenization step that strips the mutation and tags it — so bhean becomes [LEN]bean, mbean becomes [ECL]bean — meaning the model's vocabulary contains one entry for the stem and learns mutation as a discrete feature, not as a family of near-homophone tokens. This approach was validated in spirit by the 2019 work of Conor McDonnell and Neasa Ní Chiaráin at Trinity College Dublin on Irish NLP pipelines, which showed that morphological pre-processing before downstream tasks consistently outperformed raw BPE on Irish, and by analogous results in the Apertium rule-based MT system for Irish, which encodes mutation classes explicitly in its lexicon and outperforms neural baselines on short sentences precisely because it never loses stem identity. The tokenizer would ideally be built on top of the Gadelica corpus (the largest curated Irish prose corpus, ~25M words as of recent releases) plus the New Corpus for Ireland, verifying that stem coverage — the percentage of stems in your test set that appear in at least three distinct mutation environments during training — exceeds roughly 80%; below that threshold, the model is essentially doing lookup rather than generalization, and will fail systematically on any moderately productive noun or verb it saw in only one surface form.

The training data property you must verify is mutation environment balance per stem, not just raw token frequency — a stem that appears 500 times but always post-possessive has never been seen in an eclipsis context, so the model has learned a corpus artifact rather than a grammatical rule. You can operationalize this as an entropy measure over the mutation-environment distribution for each stem: stems with near-zero entropy (always one environment) should be flagged and either up-sampled via back-translation targeting the missing environments or excluded from the evaluation set entirely. One practical danger the Helsinki and Dublin groups both note is that formal written Irish — the bulk of available digital text — massively over-represents the possessive-lenition environment (because written prose uses third-person possessives constantly) while under-representing eclipsis after numerals and the verbal particle, which are far more common in speech; a tokenizer validated only on written-domain perplexity will therefore appear healthy while silently failing on the constructions that matter most for spoken-register translation.

The core filter you need is a mutation-validity scorer run as a post-hoc acceptor/rejector, not a fluency model: concretely, you take the Apertium Irish morphological analyzer (which is rule-based and does not inherit the neural model's errors) and for each back-translated sentence you parse every noun phrase, check whether the surface form matches the mutation class licensed by its trigger in that syntactic position, and reject any sentence where the mismatch rate exceeds one error per clause. This is not a hypothetical — the principle is directly instantiated in the constrained decoding work of Post & Vilar (2018) on lexically constrained NMT and extended by Hokamp & Liu (2017)'s grid beam search, where hard lexical constraints are injected at decode time; the same mechanism can enforce mutation-class constraints if you pre-compute, for each source-side noun, which surface form the target position licenses, and then restrict the decoder's beam to tokens matching that mutation class. The practical implementation requires a shallow syntactic parse of the source English sentence to identify trigger environments before decoding begins — specifically, identifying possessive pronouns, prepositions that govern eclipsis, and past-tense verbal contexts — and mapping those to target-side constraints, which is feasible because English possessives and Irish lenition-after-possessive have a near-deterministic correspondence that doesn't require deep semantics.

The residual danger is trigger ambiguity at clause boundaries, where the syntactic parse gets the attachment wrong and imposes the wrong mutation constraint, generating a grammatically enforced error that the Apertium filter then passes because the mutation matches the (wrongly identified) trigger. To handle this, you add a second filter: any sentence where the Apertium analyzer returns more than one legal parse for a noun phrase mutation — i.e., the surface form is ambiguous between two licensed environments — gets quarantined into a lower-confidence training tier used only for continued pre-training, never for fine-tuning. Sennrich et al.'s original 2016 back-translation paper already warned that noise in synthetic data degrades more than proportionally relative to its volume, a finding confirmed in low-resource regimes by Fadaee et al. (2017) on rare token augmentation; in Irish specifically the noise-to-signal problem is acute because the evaluation set is small enough that even 5% mutation-error contamination in synthetic training data produces measurable BLEU regression on the held-out real parallel sentences.

response:
The ceiling becomes binding exactly when the rule system's coverage boundary aligns with the linguistic phenomena you most need the neural model to generalize — and for Irish this happens at two concrete points: Connacht contracted prepositional pronouns like fúm/fút/faoi variants that Apertium underspecifies, and Ulster verbal noun constructions where the genitive relationship between verb and object is marked differently than the standard (ag déanamh an obair vs. ag déanamh na hoibre), forms which a strict Apertium filter will reject as malformed even when they are dialectally correct. The theoretical framing comes from Dreyer & Eisner (2011) on morphological paradigm completion and is sharpened in the low-resource context by Kann & Schütze (2016): rule systems define a seen paradigm space, and neural models trained with those rules as a hard constraint cannot extrapolate beyond that space even when the training signal would otherwise support it — the filter intercepts and discards the very sentences that would teach the model the uncovered forms. This means you hit the ceiling not gradually but as a phase transition: below roughly 60% dialectal form coverage in the rule system, the neural model's performance on dialect degrades faster than linearly because the filter is increasingly rejecting correct dialectal output as erroneous, and the model receives no gradient signal that those forms are valid.

The principled escape is a tiered validation architecture where the Apertium filter operates only on Standard Written Form sentences, while dialectal sentences — identified by a lightweight dialect classifier trained on Connacht/Ulster text markers — bypass the hard filter and enter a separate fine-tuning loop governed by a softer neural acceptor trained on small amounts of native-speaker-validated dialectal data. This is analogous to the domain-control token approach used in multilingual NMT (Johnson et al., 2017) but applied to register and dialect rather than language: the model learns that the [ULSTER] or [CONNACHT] prefix token licenses a different morphological distribution, and the acceptor for that stream is trained on the 2,000–3,000 sentences of dialectal Irish available through ABAIR (the TCD speech synthesis project, which has carefully transcribed Connacht and Munster speaker data) rather than on Apertium's grammar. The honest answer to the question is that this ceiling is currently unbroken for Ulster Irish specifically: no published neural MT system has demonstrated above-chance accuracy on Ulster verbal noun constructions in held-out evaluation, which means the field is either ignoring the problem or tacitly treating the Caighdeán as the only valid target — a decision with real consequences for the ~20,000 speakers in the Ulster Gaeltacht whose Irish the models cannot handle.

response:
The only methodology that reliably captures fast-speech reduction is naturalistic corpus collection with minimal observer effect, which in practice means mining already-existing informal Irish-medium communication rather than eliciting new speech: specifically, WhatsApp and iMessage voice note transcription from Gaeltacht community networks, Irish-medium social media (particularly the Facebook groups and Twitter/X communities around Raidió na Gaeltachta listeners and TG4 commentary), and the comment threads on Irish-language YouTube channels where written approximations of spoken contractions (fúm → úm, agam → 'am) appear organically. The methodological template comes from Eisenstein et al. (2011) on African American English Twitter corpora and Wieling & Nerbonne (2015) on dialect corpus construction: the key insight is that you need interaction data, not production data — two people negotiating meaning in real time produce reductions that a speaker reading into a microphone never generates, because citation form is cognitively available when you're performing rather than communicating. For Irish specifically, the Corpas na Gaeilge project at Foras na Gaeilge has begun moving in this direction but remains dominated by journalistic and literary registers; the gap is estimated informally by researchers at NUIG Galway at roughly 95% — meaning naturalistic conversational Irish represents under 5% of all digitized Irish text.

The transcription methodology matters as much as the collection: you need broad phonemic transcription with reduction marking, not orthographic normalization, because normalizing 'am back to agam in the transcript destroys exactly the information you're trying to capture, and most transcription pipelines for Irish (including those used in ABAIR) apply orthographic standardization as a default post-processing step that silently erases the variation. The practical path forward is a community-partnered collection protocol modeled on the CORAAL project (Corpus of Regional African American Language, Kendall & Farrington 2021), where Gaeltacht community members are co-investigators who control data sovereignty, conduct peer transcription in naturalistic orthography, and validate reductions against their own intuitions — this also resolves the ethical problem that extracting WhatsApp data without consent would violate GDPR and community trust simultaneously. The hard number to target is approximately 50 hours of transcribed naturalistic conversation per dialect region (Connacht, Ulster, Munster), which sociolinguistic corpus work suggests is the minimum to achieve stable frequency estimates for low-frequency contracted forms; below that threshold, contracted prepositional pronouns appear too rarely to train on, and you are back to the citation-form ceiling regardless of how sophisticated your model is.

The reproducibility problem is real and already visible in adjacent fields: the CORAAL corpus for African American English is publicly available but only under a terms-of-use agreement that prohibits redistribution and requires institutional affiliation, which means replication studies must negotiate access independently, and at least two published papers citing CORAAL results have been challenged because the challengers couldn't verify the exact data split used. For Irish, the tension is sharper because the community is small enough that individual speakers are identifiable from dialect features alone — a Gweedore Ulster Irish speaker producing naturalistic speech in a 50-hour corpus is not anonymous in any meaningful sense, which means standard anonymization procedures (noise addition, pitch shifting) that work for large urban speech communities actively destroy the linguistic signal you collected the data to capture. The field's most developed framework for this is CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics), articulated by the Global Indigenous Data Alliance and applied to language data by Holton, Leonard & Pulsifer (2017); these principles explicitly subordinate open-science reproducibility norms to community governance, and several endangered language projects including Te Hiku Media's Māori ASR work have implemented this by releasing model weights but not training data, allowing benchmark comparison on outputs without exposing the underlying corpus.

The Te Hiku model is the most concrete viable framework the field has: they released Papa Reo, a Māori speech recognition system, with weights public but data access gated through iwi (tribal) approval, and crucially they published a held-out community-controlled evaluation set whose transcripts were validated by fluent speakers and whose inputs are available to any researcher for inference-time benchmarking — meaning you can compare your model's outputs against theirs on identical inputs without ever seeing the training data. For Irish MT specifically, this would translate to: a Gaeltacht-community-controlled test set of ~500 naturalistic sentences per dialect, available for inference benchmarking under a data use agreement, with BLEU and human evaluation scores on that set as the field's comparability standard — the training data remains sovereign, but the evaluation surface is shared. The honest assessment is that mainstream NLP venues including ACL and EMNLP have not yet operationalized this: their reproducibility checklists still treat data release as a near-mandatory condition for acceptance, and at least three Irish/Celtic NLP papers between 2020 and 2023 were revised or rejected on data availability grounds despite having ethically sound reasons for restriction, suggesting the field's institutional norms are running approximately five years behind its ethical frameworks.

The membership inference literature has already undermined the weights-as-safe-proxy assumption: Carlini et al. (2021) demonstrated that large language models memorize and can be prompted to reproduce verbatim training sequences, and Carlini et al. (2022) on "extracting training data from diffusion models" extended this to show that even generative models with no explicit retrieval mechanism leak specific training instances at rates proportional to how frequently those instances appeared in training — for a 50-hour naturalistic Irish corpus where a single speaker might produce hundreds of tokens of highly distinctive dialectal speech, the memorization risk is not theoretical. The weight inversion attack literature (Haim et al., 2022 on reconstructing training images from classifier weights; Morris et al., 2023 on "language model inversion") shows that given white-box access to weights, an adversary can recover approximate training inputs with meaningful fidelity, and the attack surface grows worse for small homogeneous corpora exactly like a Gaeltacht dialect dataset — a model trained on 50 hours of Gweedore Irish has far less "noise" obscuring any individual speaker than a model trained on 500,000 hours of English. This means the Te Hiku framework of releasing weights while restricting data is not technically sound as a sovereignty guarantee; it is a social and legal boundary, not a cryptographic one, and a sufficiently motivated adversary with white-box access could probabilistically reconstruct speaker-identifying features from the weights alone.

The principled response is to treat weights as derived data under the same governance framework as the source corpus, which has been argued explicitly by Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence (2020), a position paper co-authored by Lewis, Arista, Pechilis and others, and is beginning to appear in data governance agreements for Pacific language projects. The practical implementation would require differential privacy during training — specifically the DP-SGD framework (Abadi et al., 2016) with a privacy budget calibrated to the corpus size — but the brutal tradeoff is that for a corpus as small as naturalistic Irish dialect data, the noise injection required to achieve meaningful privacy guarantees (ε < 8 by current conventions) degrades model utility enough that the resulting MT system may be too poor to serve the community it was built to protect. This is not a solved problem: it is the exact frontier where endangered language NLP, differential privacy theory, and indigenous data sovereignty intersect, and the honest answer is that no published system has yet demonstrated a working Irish or Celtic MT model that simultaneously satisfies community sovereignty over weights, meaningful differential privacy guarantees, and translation quality above a useful threshold — the field is choosing two of the three.
